To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

smooth armchair graphene nanoribons have smaller conductances than copper wires with unity length to width aspect ratios for widths smaller than 8 nm, and that rough edges can substantially increase the resistance of GNRs.

smooth armchair and zig-zag GNR interconnect with a width of 1.5 nm and 3 nm respectively have resistivities that are smaller than that of copper wires with unity length-to-width ratios, but rougher GNR edges can increase their resistances by an order of a magnitude.
the conductance of armchair GNRs with widths less than 4 nm and zigzag GNRs with 2 nm widths are smaller than those of copper wires with unity length-to-width aspect ratios.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the electronic properties of graphene nanoribons (GNRs).
the study of the electronic and transport properties of graphene nanoribons (GNRs).
the development of compact physics-based equivalent circuit models for graphene nanoribbon interconnects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
GNRs can provide an excellent alternative to copper for interconnects with widths smaller than 8 nm.
GNRs are a viable interconnect candidate for the 10 nm technology node and beyond.
the use of graphene nanoribons as interconnects in integrated circuits would be advantageous only if the GNRs are very wide, very short, or very thin.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
GNRs can be used to replace Cu interconnects for on-chip wiring at widths below 8nm and at aspect ratios below unity.
, for narrow GNRs, the resistance per unit length can be smaller than Cu, but for wider GNRs, it can be larger than Cu.
the physics-based equivalent circuit models presented herein provide a useful design tool for the design and optimization of GNR interconnect structures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the resistances of GNRs are comparable with those of Cu wires for narrow widths, but the resistivities are lower.
GNRs are promising candidates for future interconnect applications, and that the physics-based circuit models can be used as a tool to optimize the GNR geometry for a given interconnect application.
GNRs can be a viable candidate for interconnects in the near future.
